raw_case_text:
A six-year-old girl with CKD (single kidney, congenital) undergoing peritoneal dialysis presented with fever and a lesion suggestive of linear erythema throughout the marginal gingiva. The patient reported pain in the gingival region and difficulty eating and drinking.
The initial diagnosis was pneumonia with febrile neutropenia and hypoalbuminemia. Due to the clinical condition, the patient was admitted to pediatric ICU. After a few days of hospitalization, the entire length of the marginal and attached gingiva, both on the buccal and palatal sides, showed white coloration suggestive of necrosis (Figure 1). No dental caries was observed.
A fragment of the marginal gingiva was collected for screening culture, in which the presence of P. aeruginosa was detected. As the pathogen was also detected in blood and nasal secretion cultures, the case was diagnosed as septic shock.
Systemic antibiotic therapy was started (vancomycin, ampicillin-sulbactam, amikacin, piperacillin-tazobactam and polymyxin B) and after a period of hospitalization, a gradual elimination of necrotic gingival mucosa was observed. A hard tissue with bone appearance was present in the remaining normal gingiva, but presented as a fragile structure (Figure 2).
Pathological tooth mobility was present as well as bone loss especially between the first permanent molars and incisors both in the upper and lower jaws (Figure 3). There was clinical insertion loss but without periodontal pockets (Figure 2).
Supragingival scraping sessions and application of 0.12% chlorhexidine were performed during the ICU stay. After biopsy of the gingival tissue and the exposed hard tissue, the presence of inflammatory hyperplastic gingivitis was confirmed and the hard tissue was confirmed as bone tissue (Figures 4 and 5). The bone tissue was submitted to culture, which also showed the presence of P. aeruginosa. Systemic antibiotic therapy based on levofloxacin was established for another fifteen days.
Bone lesions and some deciduous teeth with high mobility were surgically removed, under antibiotic prophylaxis; antibiotic therapy was maintained postoperatively for seven days. The collected material was sent for histopathology and culture examinations (Figure 6).
Histopathology showed a chronic inflammatory process in necrotic tissue, resulting in the diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis. P. aeruginosa was not detected in culture examination.
Fifteen days later, the patient had significant oral health improvement (Figure 7). After the six-month treatment period, the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was detected, although the patient had negative serology in previous tests.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old girl with congenital single kidney and chronic kidney disease undergoing peritoneal dialysis presenting with fever, gingival erythema, and oral pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 6-year-old girl with chronic kidney disease on peritoneal dialysis presented with fever and a linear erythematous lesion throughout the marginal gingiva, associated with gingival pain and difficulty eating and drinking. She was initially diagnosed with pneumonia with febrile neutropenia and hypoalbuminemia, necessitating admission to the pediatric intensive care unit. During hospitalization, the marginal and attached gingiva on both buccal and palatal aspects developed white necrotic discoloration, followed by exposed fragile bone-like tissue, pathological tooth mobility, and severe bone loss without periodontal pockets.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital single kidney; chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing peritoneal dialysis; history of negative serology on previous testing.
subjective.review_of_systems: Gingival pain, difficulty eating and drinking; absence of dental caries.

objective.physical_examination: Pediatric ICU admission. Oral/Gingival examination: Linear erythema throughout the marginal gingiva; subsequent development of white coloration suggestive of necrosis along the entire length of marginal and attached gingiva on buccal and palatal sides; no dental caries; fragile bone-like hard tissue exposed in remaining gingiva; pathological tooth mobility; clinical insertion loss without periodontal pockets.
objective.advanced_workup: Gingival tissue and exposed hard tissue biopsy: Inflammatory hyperplastic gingivitis and bone tissue; histopathology of resected bone lesions showed chronic inflammatory process in necrotic tissue, diagnostic of chronic osteomyelitis. Radiographic examination showed bone loss between the first permanent molars and incisors in upper and lower jaws.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Newly detected human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (diagnosed after a 6-month treatment period following previously negative serology) complicated by septic shock secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa (isolated from marginal gingiva, blood, nasal secretion, and bone tissue), pneumonia, and chronic mandibular/maxillary osteomyelitis with necrotic gingivitis.
Clinical Plan & Outcome: Initial ICU management included supragingival scraping, topical 0.12% chlorhexidine, and systemic antibiotics (vancomycin, ampicillin-sulbactam, amikacin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and polymyxin B). Subsequent targeted therapy included levofloxacin for 15 days, surgical debridement of bone lesions, and extraction of mobile deciduous teeth under antibiotic prophylaxis (continued for 7 days postoperatively). Histopathology confirmed chronic osteomyelitis (repeat culture negative for P. aeruginosa). The patient showed marked oral health improvement 15 days post-surgery.
